claim: Stopping when accumulated agreement among samples passes a threshold cuts samples by about 3x on average with under 0.1 points accuracy loss (Adaptive-Consistency, 17 datasets, 3 models, cap 40). Checked against the paper: math 73.2 vs 73.1, 40 vs 13.8 samples.
agent_test: At equal mean tokens, compare fixed-N majority vote to Beta-posterior stop (threshold .95, cap 40) on our task set; report accuracy and mean samples per item.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A window rule (stop when the last w answers agree; w=5, w=8 for MATH) cuts samples by 34 to 84 percent versus fixed self-consistency with accuracy within 0.02 to 0.85 points. Checked: GPT-4 GSM8K 7.98 of 40 samples, GPT-3.5 14.65, Llama-2 7B MATH 62.48 of 64.
agent_test: Run window-5 stop against Beta stop and fixed N=10 at matched tokens; check the accuracy drop on hard items.

claim: In a head-to-head comparison (Aggarwal et al. 2023) the Beta, Dirichlet and Chinese-restaurant-process stopping rules reach similar savings while Beta beats entropy and majority-only at equal cost and random stopping is worst; SPRT (ConSol), difficulty-prior (DSC) and quality-weighted (RASC) stopping each report 56-86% cost or token savings versus self-consistency, but on different models and benchmarks and not compared against one another.
agent_test: Replay stored answers through Beta, window and SPRT rules and compare accuracy at cost matched to 1.0x, 0.5x and 0.3x of fixed N.
audit_note: Only Aggarwal et al. compare stopping rules head to head (Beta, Dirichlet, CRP similar; Beta consistently beats entropy and majority; random worst); SPRT (ConSol), difficulty prior (DSC) and RASC are separate papers on different models and benchmarks with different savings (up to 84.8-86.2% tokens, 56-65% cost, ~70% samples), so 'similar savings' across all five rules is not shown.
claim_before_audit: Different stopping rules (Beta, entropy, SPRT, window, difficulty prior) reach similar savings; random stopping is worst and majority-only is mostly worse at equal cost.

claim: Using question difficulty or prior information to set the starting allocation saves a further 22 to 25 percent over ESC (DSC, 6 benchmarks). The 3.8 percent figure (questions that benefit from SC) is not checked beyond the abstract.
agent_test: Add a one-sample triage: if the first two answers agree on an easy-labeled item, stop; compare with uniform start at equal tokens.

claim: Weighting votes by model confidence reaches the same accuracy with fewer samples or tokens: P(True)-weighted voting (CISC) cut samples by 41% at 5 and 46% at 10 samples on average (some settings over 67%), and trace-confidence filtering (DeepConf) cut tokens by 18-85% depending on variant, with the aggressive variant sometimes losing accuracy; between-question calibration (ECE, Brier) does not predict the gain, within-question discrimination does.
agent_test: Compare unweighted vote, confidence-weighted vote and confidence-filtered stop at equal tokens; measure within-question AUROC of our confidence prompt.
audit_note: 40 to 85 percent mixes CISC's average 41-46% sample reduction (some cells over 67%) with DeepConf's best-case 84.7% token cut; DeepConf savings run 15-85% depending on setting and its aggressive variant can lose accuracy, so 'same accuracy with 40 to 85 percent fewer' is too uniform.
claim_before_audit: Weighting votes by model confidence (P(True), trace confidence) reaches the same accuracy with 40 to 85 percent fewer samples or tokens; between-question calibration does not predict the gain, within-question discrimination does.

claim: Reasoning models can stop their own chain early: exiting at a high-confidence trial answer (DEER) cuts chain length 19.1 to 80.1 percent with accuracy changes of +0.3 to +5.0 points, and on math tasks models typically converge to their final answer after about 60 percent of the reasoning steps, leaving about 40 percent of the chain after convergence.
agent_test: Probe a trial answer at each reasoning transition and stop after k consistent probes; compare accuracy against the full chain at equal tokens.
audit_note: Liu and Wang report models converge to their final answer after about 60% of reasoning steps on math, so about 40% (not 60%) of reasoning follows convergence.
claim_before_audit: Reasoning models can stop their own chain early: exiting at a high-confidence trial answer or after answer convergence cuts chain length 19 to 80 percent without lowering accuracy (often +0.3 to +5 points); about 60 percent of math reasoning is spent after the answer has converged.

claim: More samples keep helping in verifiable domains: coverage rises with samples over several orders of magnitude (SWE-bench Lite 15.9 to 56 percent from 1 to 250 samples), so the bound is a cost choice, and a verifier is needed to turn coverage into accuracy. Gap search: at equal sample count a model-verifier beat agreement (Gemini 1.5 Pro, 200 samples, MATH 467 vs 460 of 500, AIME 8 vs 4 of 15) but at 50 extra verification calls per sample, so equal-token gain is still unmeasured.
agent_test: Where a test exists, sample to a pass-bound rather than an agreement-bound; compare cost.
audit_note: Minor: 'a verifier is needed to turn coverage into accuracy' is an interpretation; Brown et al. show majority voting and reward models plateau near 100 samples.

claim: Voting gains over greedy CoT are large and grow with model scale (GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2; +3-6 on UL2-20B vs +9-23 on LaMDA-137B); weak models give a weaker majority signal.
agent_test: Re-measure vote gain on our model at N=1, 3, 10; do not assume published gains.

claim: In humans a speed-accuracy instruction moves the diffusion boundary (boundary 0.109 vs 0.152, N=14; median RT 120-200 ms longer in the accuracy regime, accuracy changing 0-6%), and 72 of 85 humans are best fit by a fixed (non-collapsing) bound; in macaques the neural termination threshold was similar across regimes (RT 176 and 159 ms longer under accuracy emphasis), with speed pressure acting through an evidence-independent urgency signal. No LLM test of a careful-versus-fast instruction against a diffusion boundary was found; closest proxies are prompt-based token budgets.
agent_test: Expose the bound (threshold or window) as an instruction-level knob and check that accuracy and tokens move as predicted.
audit_note: Numbers check out, but Hanks et al. 2014 found the monkey LIP termination threshold did NOT differ between speed and accuracy regimes (speed pressure acted via an evidence-independent urgency signal), so 'in humans and monkeys the instruction moves the bound' is wrong for monkeys; Hawkins et al. speaks to fixed vs collapsing bounds, not the instruction effect.
claim_before_audit: In humans and monkeys a speed-accuracy instruction moves the bound: boundary 0.109 vs 0.152 (N=14), RT 176 and 159 ms longer in the accuracy regime, and 72 of 85 humans fit a fixed bound best. Checked against Ratcliff and McKoon Table 1, Hanks 2014 and Hawkins 2015. Gap search: no LLM test of a careful-vs-fast instruction against a diffusion boundary was found; closest proxies are prompt-based token budgets (K26).

claim: Whether the bound collapses over time is contested: 72 of 85 humans prefer a fixed bound, but 4 of 8 monkeys prefer collapsing (2 fixed, 2 urgency); theory says the optimal bound collapses under mixed difficulty; the result depends on between-trial variability and training. Gap search: theory source (Shadlen and Kiani 2013) says flat bounds are optimal only for known, stationary reliability; Chen 2024 shows fixed-N voting turns worse on hard items. No LLM test of fixed vs collapsing bound was found.
agent_test: Compare a fixed agreement threshold with one that relaxes as samples are used (cap 40) on a mixed-difficulty set at equal tokens.

claim: Raising the bound buys little accuracy for a large time cost: in humans 0 to 6 points of accuracy for 120 to 200 ms; in LLMs accuracy changes by about -0.1 at 3.3x fewer samples.
agent_test: Plot accuracy against samples on our tasks and set the cap where gain falls under 1 point per 10 percent extra tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the -0.1 at 3.3x fewer samples is the maths category (73.2 to 73.1); the all-category average is -0.04, and the LLM comparison is a lowered adaptive bound vs fixed 40 samples.

claim: LLM samples are correlated, not independent, so a binomial or Beta stopping rule over-trusts agreement. Measured accuracy drops at the .95 bound are small (-0.1 to -0.2) but consistent wrong answers are not removed. Gap search: still no measured confident-wrong rate; Brown 2024 shows consensus-wrong on problems where correct answers are rare, and Yue 2024 shows mixed prompts separate easy from hard better.
agent_test: Measure the rate of confident-wrong stops; compare same-prompt and diversified-prompt samples at equal tokens.

claim: Savings shrink on hard sets: ESC used 62.5 of 64 samples for Llama-2 7B on MATH and 42.4 of 64 for GPT-4 on MATH; hard items run to the cap.
agent_test: Report samples used per difficulty bin and confirm the cap is paid only on hard items.
audit_note: Minor: the 62.5 and 42.4 are averages of 64 (Llama-2 7B accuracy 7.68 on MATH); 'hard items run to the cap' is an inference from averages, not per-item data. RASC (Abstract Algebra 8.54 vs 6.15 College Math samples) gives a second consistent data point.

claim: A decision-model controller for stop, verify or abandon did not raise agent success: cost per attempt x1.19 (CI 1.02-1.36) at the same 73.0 percent pass rate on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21 tasks, 315 trials); finish ranking AUROC 0.78 but calibration poor (0.50 predicted vs 87 percent passed).
schema_part: S9 finish rule (no extra controller layer)
agent_test: Test the schema finish rule against a no-controller baseline at equal tokens; require a pass-rate gain, not only a ranking gain.

claim: Reasoning-trace length aligns with human reaction time: partial r with log human RT is 0.552 for GPT-OSS-120B and 0.197 for non-reasoning DeepSeek-V3; multiple-path decoding raises alignment for some models only (R1 gain not significant).
agent_test: Use trace length or samples-to-bound as a difficulty signal and test whether it predicts failure (AUROC) on our items.

claim: Opt-out options gave no accuracy gain in human perceptual decisions (0.82 vs 0.82, N=24; 0.83 vs 0.84, N=26; N=36 null), so letting the agent skip items needs a measured benefit.
agent_test: Test an abstain option on our agent: does abstaining lift accuracy on answered items at equal total tokens?

claim: Human thinking time tracks expected benefit of computation in chess (519 million moves; square-root form beat linear, dAIC 3.6e8), as value-of-computation theory predicts.
agent_test: Allocate attempts by estimated gain per item and compare with uniform allocation at equal tokens.

claim: Fitted bound values depend on the model: boundary recovery R2 drops from .99 to .77 and boundary separation is overestimated when Levy-flight data are fit with a Wiener DDM (Hato et al. 2025). Separately, adding trial-level (systematic) drift predictors improved WAIC from 114,803 to 37,537 in a recognition-memory dataset (Sun et al. 2026), showing that the standard model is a poor fit, though that paper does not report resulting bound shifts.
agent_test: Report stop-rule results with two aggregators and treat parameter values as model-specific.
audit_note: Hato et al. support bound dependence on model (R2 .99 to .77, boundary overestimated under misspecification), but the 114,803 to 37,537 WAIC figure (Sun et al.) is a model-fit improvement from adding trial-level predictors, not evidence that fitted bound values change.
claim_before_audit: Fitted bound values depend on the model: boundary recovery R2 drops from .99 to .77 when Levy-flight data are fit with a Wiener DDM; allowing systematic drift variability changes WAIC from 114,803 to 37,537. Published bound numbers are model-dependent.

claim: At equal sample count, picking by repeated model self-verification beat picking by agreement (Gemini 1.5 Pro, 200 samples: AIME 8 vs 4 of 15, LiveBench Reasoning 97 vs 75 of 140), while agreement and off-the-shelf reward models both plateau near 100 samples (MATH Llama-3-8B majority 40.50 to 41.41 percent from 100 to 10,000 samples vs coverage 82.9 to 98.44). Equal-token comparison is not measured (verification used 50 calls per sample).
schema_part: O3 stop signal: verifier before agreement where one exists
agent_test: Run the agreement bound and a test-pass bound on code tasks at equal total tokens (including verifier calls); report accuracy per 1k tokens.
audit_note: Only Zhao et al. show a verifier (model self-verification) beating agreement at equal sample count; Brown et al. find reward models plateau like majority voting (40.50 to 41.41 range) and Setlur et al. compare verifier-based vs verifier-free fine-tuning, not selection at equal sample count, so 'tests, ... reward-based' beating agreement is not shown.
claim_before_audit: At equal sample COUNT, picking by a verifier (tests, model self-verification, reward-based) beats picking by agreement, and agreement plateaus near 100 samples while coverage keeps rising: MATH Llama-3-8B majority 40.50 to 41.41 percent from 100 to 10,000 samples vs coverage 82.9 to 98.44; Gemini 1.5 Pro at 200 samples AIME 8 vs 4 of 15, LiveBench Reasoning 97 vs 75 of 140. Equal-TOKEN comparison is not measured (verification used 50 calls per sample).

claim: Agreement stops on a consistent wrong answer by structure: when the right answer is rare (minority), more votes make the wrong consensus win more often. Fixed-N voting is non-monotone with mixed difficulty (accuracy up then down on MMLU Physics, GPQA, TruthfulQA, AVeriTeC); one AIME problem had 1 correct in 200 samples. No numerical rate of agreement-bound stops that were wrong was reported by any source.
schema_part: O3 cap + G (vary prompts between samples)
agent_test: Log every stop and its correctness on a hard set; report the share of stops (agreement at or above .95) whose answer was wrong, by difficulty bin.
audit_note: Minor: Chen et al. show non-monotone curves 'often' on the four datasets (Vote rises then falls on MMLU Physics; Filter-Vote does the reverse), not uniformly up-then-down on all four; the absence claim about error-rate numbers cannot be verified from sources.

claim: A verifier-based stop also fails: unit tests give false positives that rise with attempts K; with a cost for a wrong accept the best K is often under 10 (about 5 at cost-benefit ratio 4, HumanEval+/MBPP) and can be zero. Model families differ (Llama-3.1-70B steep, Code Llama gradual).
agent_test: Compare the test-pass rate on our checker against a stricter held-out check; set K from that false-positive rate.

claim: Agreement bound on current long-chain open reasoning models: the 0.95 weighted-vote stop with a 16-trace warmup and cap 512 saved 18 to 85 percent of tokens versus full voting with accuracy within about 1 point for the conservative variant; looser bounds (0.90, 0.85) saved up to 69.6 percent but cost accuracy in the aggressive variant. Accuracy drops: Qwen3-8B AIME25 -4.4 points. Authors name overconfident wrong traces as the key limit. Only one paper tests this on reasoning models at scale (plus ConSol).
schema_part: O3 stop rule on reasoning models
agent_test: Replicate on our own model: 16 warmup samples, stop at .95, cap 64; report tokens and accuracy vs full majority.

claim: Varying the prompt style between samples (chain of thought plus program of thought) separated easy from hard questions better than same-prompt agreement, letting a cascade reach 0.929 accuracy at 40 percent of strong-model cost. It is the only prompt-diversity result; it reports routing quality, not a confident-wrong rate.
agent_test: Compare same-prompt vs mixed-prompt agreement for the share of confident-wrong stops.

claim: For open-ended output (summaries, free-form QA, SQL) the model can select the most consistent sample (universal self-consistency); it matches exact-match voting where both apply (GSM8K 90.2 vs 90.4) but provides no confidence level and is capped by context length, so no sequential bound has been shown outside closed answers.
agent_test: Test a pairwise-agreement bound on drafts of a plan or write-up; check against human rating.

claim: Fidelity of our Beta/SPRT mapping: SPRT accumulates log likelihood ratio to two bounds (Wald; Shadlen and Kiani 2013), and flat bounds are optimal only when the evidence-to-logLR conversion is known or evidence is stationary. The diffusion decision model's boundary a is a distance in accumulated-evidence units, not defined as logLR, and its authors say criterion setting is not explained. Gold and Shadlen 2007 and Ratcliff 1978 themselves were not opened; the reviews above stand in.
schema_part: Method note for O3 (Beta bound is a Bayesian choice)
agent_test: State in the schema that the agreement bound is a heuristic SPRT with unknown per-sample reliability; add a cap.
audit_note: Minor: 'boundary a is a distance in accumulated-evidence units, not defined as logLR' is an inference; Ratcliff and McKoon define it as the evidence needed to decide, and state that diffusion analyses do not explain how criteria are set.

claim: Prompt instructions can move how much an LLM reasons, with measured accuracy: Chain of Draft (5 words per step) kept CoT accuracy (coin flip 100 percent both; date 88.1 vs 90.2 for GPT-4o) with as little as 7.6 percent of tokens but not on models under 3B; a token budget in the prompt cut output 67 percent but a too-small budget raised token use; forcing continuation with Wait lifted AIME24 50 to 57 percent. None compares to a diffusion boundary or reports cost per accuracy point.
agent_test: Run the same items under fast, default and careful instructions; report tokens and accuracy and fit a cost per point.
audit_note: Minor: the GPT-4o date CoD/CoT rows are mis-ordered in text extraction but consistent with 88.1 vs 90.2; TALE-EP's 67% token cut came with an accuracy drop (81.03 vs 83.75).

claim: Spending samples by difficulty works: a per-difficulty strategy matched best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (MATH, PaLM 2-S*), difficulty from the model's own pass rate beat human labels, and weak-model agreement as the difficulty signal cut cost to 40 percent at equal accuracy. Which cheap signal is best (first-two agreement, trace length, confidence) has not been compared head to head.
agent_test: Compare first-two-sample agreement, trace length and confidence as bound-setters on one item set at equal tokens.
audit_note: Abstract says efficiency improved by more than 4x vs best-of-N; 14x and 40 percent cost confirmed; 'matched' wording is close.
